messages.author: 958272119e13f0e7
messages.subject: Climatology + anomaly
parts:
Hi,

We are looking for an example of fitting a space-time climatology and
anomaly fields with INLA.

To explain what I mean by this, consider a large collection of sea
surface temperature measurements spread across e.g the North Atlantic
for many years. Temperature shows a strong spatial pattern and temporal
variability on (at least) two time-scales - a seasonal cycle (winter vs
summer) and also interannual variability (e.g. due to climate change)

The model that I would like to fit is therefore of the style

T ~ c(x,y,t1) + a(x,y,t2) + e

where
* T are the temperature observations
* c(x,y,t1) is a seasonal climatology, giving the average temperature as
a function of the day of year (t1), and, looping on 1 Jan
* a(x,y,t2) is the anomaly field, giving the temperature anomaly
relative to the climatology for all of the time points (t2) in our data
set. e.g. from 1 Jan 1960 to 1 Jan 2017. The mean of this anomaly field
should be zero.

The time resolution of t1 and t2 need not be the same, and I suspect
that computational limitations will probably mean that they are not.

Does anyone know of any comparable examples that we could use to help us
develop such a model?

Thanks,

Philipp and Mark
--

messages.subject: Re: Climatology + anomaly
parts:
Hi,

I am currently doing something vaguely similar on  extremes of global temperature data, where  spatial and regional trends are decomposed into the spatial climatology (fixed over time) and certain linear and nonlinear time trend components with sum-to-zero constraints. I can send you some slides on this from a recent presentation if you are interested. If you need a spatial field for each day of your observation period, I think that the dimension of the latent model would be huge. It will depend a lot on what kind of structure you want to put into the anomaly function ...

Thomas

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: Climatology + anomaly
parts:
For daily timescales, you quickly exceed the reasonable range of what the R-INLA package can do.  With a bit of non-stationarity, the most I've done is about 30 time points, which doesn't go a very long way. I'm currently working on a large EU project on daily temperature reconstruction since 1850, using stations, ships, and satellites. There are 10^11 latent variables in the combined weather and climate processes.  When going to those kinds of scales, one cannot do Cholesky factorisations of the whole system, which is required by inla, and iterative solver methods are needed, with lots of techniques for multiscale preconditioning. This  changes the practical implementation quite a lot. (We are also not even trying to do a fully Bayesian analysis for the model parameters.)

In the future, we'll hopefully have the resources required to gather these kinds of methods in to a second generation INLA package, but it's not easy to make general implementations; the specific model structure can have a big impact on how the computations need to be structured.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Climatology + anomaly
parts:
Now, adding some comments specific to your problem.
Since you're not working globally, there are possibilities.

First, as you imply, you likely don't need daily timescale for the seasonal field; it should vary fairly smoothly over time, so quadratic b-spline basis function in time, with a few days or even a month between the knots should be ok.
This is the technique I use for the global problem as well, but unfortunately I don't have anything written in a form that's ready to be released outside the project right now. I do have slides from presentations about the general approach.

The basic space-time construction in the Cameletti et al paper might be helpful,
but you'll likely find that your daily timescale would require a ridiculous amount of memory if run as a single batch in inla. There are options for using smaller inla runs as building blocks for the full solution, but that's ongoing research.

Finn
